newsitem.title: UK: Dlr and stg grind out new highs vs mark in Europe.
newsitem.headline: Dlr and stg grind out new highs vs mark in Europe.

text.p: The dollar and sterling edged higher on Wednesday against a beleagured mark, hamstrung by intense speculation about a broad-based start to European monetary union and perceived Bundesbank ambivalence to its fall.
Traders said buying of dollars for European currencies in general was also noted throughout the day.
Dollar/mark touched its highest level since February 1994 and was helped in part by sterling/mark's nudge to new 6-years ahead of an expected rise in UK interest rates on Thursday.
The mark also fell to its lowest level against the Japanese yen in almost two years, reflecting generalised yen strength.
"To some extent this has become a weak mark story and in the absence of anything new the market's been playing that game," said Adrian Schmidt, economist at Chase Investment Bank.
"Today has been pretty quiet on the news front, however, and I think we will probably need something else to take us above the 1994 (dollar/mark) high."
At 1540 GMT, the dollar was trading at 1.7605/12 marks compared with 1.7573/78 late Tuesday and a new 41-month high set earlier at 1.7655. The peak from February 1994 was 1.7686.
Sterling/mark, meantime, was at 2.9671/81 compared with 2.9685/92 late yesterday and a new six-year high at 2.9760.

Growing speculation about a wide memberhsip of the new European single currency from its inception in 1999 has been illustrated by the collapse in the 10-year yield spread between Italian and German bonds to under one percentage point for the first time this week. It fell further today to 93 basis points.
Analysts said this undermines the German unit because of concerns about the stability of the euro that will replace it.

The steady slide of the mark this year has met with little or no vocal protest from the Bundesbank, meantime. This may be encouraging market players to test the limits of the traditionally hawkish central bank's tolerance, analysts said.
"Until the Bundesbank shows some concern, the market will continue to take the mark lower," said Paul Meggyesi, senior currency economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.
Others feel the mark may be in for a bit of a breather and at least a temporary topping out of the dollar/mark at the 1994 highs could be the catalyst.

Schmidt at Chase said the dollar has lost a lot of its interest rate support amid a scaling back of Federal Reserve tightening expectations. There is a high correlation between dollar/mark and moves in the 10-year U.S./German yield spreads and this spread has shrunk sharply in recent weeks.
The sterling/mark rise to new highs has also been a catalyst in buoying the dollar/mark and keeping the mark generally depressed, traders said.

While sterling has been in demand ahead of Thursday's Bank of England monetary policy council meeting, traders are not convinced further gains in the pound are likely on the announcement of anything less than a half-point rate rise.

"A quarter-point rate rise is so discounted in sterling at this stage that the risk has got to be for a sell-off if that's all we get," said a trader at a UK bank here. "A half-point would rally it, but who at the Bank wants sterling higher?"
Dollar/yen was slighty firmer on the day after Japanese May current account data was broadly in line with expectations.
However, traders said the yen remained robust and dollar/yen itself continued to trade with a bias to the downside.

Analysts said the surge of the yen since mid-May has altered Japanese overseas investment decisions and many were now less keen to search for the higher yields elsewhere now that the currency risk profile has changed. Moreover, the turbulence in many south east Asian currencies at present is seeing a repatriation of Japanese capital from the region.
--Mike Dolan, London newsroom +44 171 542 6762
